clue.text: Carrying weight after beginning to slim? Just a little

indicators.note: the weighty piece is placed after the opening letter, so it follows in the answer
the beginning of the word slim is its opening letter, which is all that is taken

parts.note: something carrying weight is important, or mattering

explanation.surface: A dieter wonders whether a little weight still counts once the slimming has begun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to' takes S from slim; 'after' puts MATTERING behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: A smattering is a slight, superficial amount of knowledge or of anything, so just a little.

clue.text: Bar? This may see ball tipped over it

definitions.meaning: as a preposition, bar means except, a sense shared by the word meaning excluding

definitions.text: This may see ball tipped over it
definitions.meaning: a goalkeeper's stop can involve tipping the ball over the crossbar

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper flicks the ball over the crossbar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' is both the preposition meaning except and, in the second reading, the crossbar the ball is tipped over.
explanation.definitionFit: Save means except as a preposition, and in football a save is the keeper stopping a goal.

clue.text: Failure to contact as a result of inadequate address?

definitions.text: Failure to contact as a result of inadequate address?

parts.words: Failure to contact as a result of inadequate address?
parts.note: looks like a letter undelivered because of a bad postal address, but in golf addressing the ball is setting up the stroke, and a bad set-up means missing the ball entirely

explanation.surface: A letter goes astray because the postal address was incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf and cricket, a stroke that misses the ball completely is called this; 'address' is the golfer's stance over the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A swing that completely misses the ball, failing to make contact, is the sporting term described.

clue.text: Not exaggerating the determination of a quiet man?

definitions.meaning: used as understatement, the phrase means putting it mildly

definitions.text: the determination of a quiet man?
definitions.meaning: a taciturn man is resolved to utter as little as possible

explanation.surface: Without overstating it, a reserved man is resolute.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom signals deliberate understatement, and read literally it is a quiet man's aim to speak minimally.

clue.text: Scoundrel runs a con-trick, offering 50 for 1000

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

indicators.note: the Roman numeral for 50 is put in place of the Roman numeral for 1000

parts.note: a scam is a swindle or confidence trick

explanation.surface: A crook pulls a swindle, giving a pittance for a large sum.
explanation.walkthrough: In Roman numerals L is 50 and M is 1000, so 'offering 50 for 1000' turns SCAM into SCAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a dishonest or mischievous person, a rogue or scoundrel.

clue.text: Go carefully — rich man shortly going to fall precipitately

parts.note: to nose forward is to move slowly and cautiously

indicators.note: cut short, so the final letter of the name is dropped

parts.note: Dives is the traditional name of the rich man in Jesus's parable of Lazarus

explanation.surface: A warning that a wealthy man is about to plunge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' trims DIVES to DIVE; 'going to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To nosedive is to plunge steeply downward, as a plane or share prices do.

clue.text: Attempt to bring cricketers back

indicators.note: bringing something back turns it round, so the cricketers' word is read from right to left

parts.note: batsmen are often called bats in cricket

explanation.surface: Someone tries to recall the players to the cricket field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns BATS into the answer; 'to bring' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a stab at something is to make an attempt at it, an informal synonym.

clue.text: Holiday visits? Our island will get millions after a brief time

indicators.note: the other pieces come after the abbreviation for time

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time, made brief
taken as written

explanation.surface: A small island expects millions of visitors after a short season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' signals that the time abbreviation leads; 'will get' is a link, and 'Holiday visits?' has a question mark because it defines loosely.
explanation.definitionFit: Tourism is the business of holiday travel, people visiting places for leisure.

clue.text: Hold-up, though not in the supply of booze

definitions.text: Hold-up, though not in the supply of booze

parts.words: Hold-up, though not in the supply of booze
parts.note: a traffic jam or delay takes its name from the narrow top of a wine container, though this one has nothing to do with drink

explanation.surface: A delay that, for once, has nothing to do with the drinks delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: The narrow part of a bottle slows the flow of its contents, hence the word for any congestion.
explanation.definitionFit: A bottleneck is a narrow point causing congestion and delay, a hold-up in traffic or production.

clue.text: Computer wreckers against adopting one trick

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so the word for against takes the other pieces inside it

parts.note: VS is short for versus, meaning against
I is the Roman numeral for one
a ruse is a trick or stratagem

explanation.surface: A villain opposes taking up a single scam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'against' as versus is a common crossword convention; 'adopting' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Computer viruses are malicious programs that damage or wreck the machines they infect.

clue.text: Observed someone leaving in a hurry, but remains in the workshop

parts.note: saw is the past tense of see, to observe
someone departing at speed leaves a cloud of dust behind them

explanation.surface: A witness watched a figure flee, though the carpenter's debris stayed put.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawdust is the fine waste left behind when wood is cut, typical leftovers in a carpenter's shop.

clue.text: As caf worker in good job, I lost position for drinking

indicators.note: a letter that is lost is taken out of the café worker's word

parts.note: a waiter works in a café
taken as written
a place is a position of employment, a job

explanation.surface: A café waiter with a good job has lost his post.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan prints 'café'. 'lost' removes I from WAITER, giving WATER.
explanation.definitionFit: A watering place is a spot where animals come to drink, or humorously a pub.

clue.text: A particular point in history?

parts.note: read cryptically, a point is a dot, and the phrase for a time long ago names a year that is just a dot

explanation.surface: A question about one specific moment in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means time immemorial, the very distant past, but the clue plays on 'point' as a literal dot.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a British idiom for an unspecified time very long ago, the beginning of history.

clue.text: Off-colour? Medicine with no little power required

indicators.note: having none of something means it is taken away from the word for medicine

parts.note: a pill is a tablet of medicine
P is the abbreviation for power in physics

explanation.surface: A sick patient is told no strong drugs are needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' removes P from PILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling off-colour is feeling slightly unwell, which is a mild synonym for being sick.

clue.text: Changing places? It is requiring particular skill

indicators.note: changing the letters of places and it is means rearranging them

explanation.surface: Swapping seats is said to call for expertise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing' rearranges PLACES and ITIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Specialist as an adjective describes work needing expert, focused knowledge rather than general ability.

clue.text: Intermittent wages restricting leader of the church

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so the word for wages surrounds the other letters

parts.note: pay is money earned, wages

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A minister's salary arrives only now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader of' takes the first letter of 'the', not of 'church'; 'restricting' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something patchy is uneven or irregular, occurring in spots, which is what intermittent describes.

clue.text: Mystery play character always confused many

parts.note: ever means always, as in 'for ever'

indicators.note: jumbled up, so the letters of the word many are rearranged

explanation.surface: An actor in a medieval drama is perpetually muddled by crowds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' gives YMAN. Everyman is strictly a morality play, close kin to the mystery plays.
explanation.definitionFit: The title figure of the medieval play Everyman represents all humanity in that religious drama.

clue.text: To unman actors, issue reproof

parts.note: the cast is the set of actors in a play
to rate someone is an old verb meaning to scold them

explanation.surface: Someone scolds actors so harshly that it saps their courage.
explanation.definitionFit: To castrate a man is literally to unman him by removing the testicles.

clue.text: Bag lady mostly receiving zero amount of work

parts.note: a case is a bag for carrying things

indicators.note: to receive is to take in, so the shortened word holds the zero inside it
most of the word, with its final letter dropped

parts.note: taken as written before shortening
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A bag lady takes in nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' gives LAD; 'receiving' puts the zero inside it. 'Bag lady' reads as a phrase but splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A caseload is the quantity of cases a professional must handle, their volume of work.

clue.text: Drunk's arrived? Tough!

parts.note: a sot is a habitual drunkard; the 's is read as is
someone who has arrived is here

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off news that the drunk has turned up.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is a defiant retort, like tough luck, ending an argument.

clue.text: No tailless blind creatures after end of carving phrased in pithy way

indicators.note: the words for no and the creatures come after the carving's final letter
the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: without a tail, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: the three blind mice of the nursery rhyme

explanation.surface: The italicised words read like a cryptic proverb about mutilated mice.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic words are themselves gnomic, as the definition says. 'end of' takes G from carving; 'tailless' cuts MICE to MIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnomic means expressed in short, pithy maxims, often obscure in meaning.

clue.text: Bullfighter, male, attending a party, attracting Maria's heart

parts.note: attending an event means being at it
a do is an informal party

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

explanation.surface: A toreador goes to a party and catches the eye of Maria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heart' takes R, the centre of Maria; 'attracting' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A matador is the principal bullfighter, who kills the bull.

clue.text: Wild cat's last in zoo — tragic case, followed by many

indicators.note: the word for many comes after the three letters
the last letter of each of the next three words is taken

parts.note: a lot means many

explanation.surface: A news story of a wild cat's sad death in a zoo, followed by crowds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last in' takes O, C, E from zoo, tragic, case; 'cat's' reads as cat is.
explanation.definitionFit: The ocelot is a spotted wild cat of Central and South America.

clue.text: Jazz fan's about to return for performance

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the letter for about goes back along the word

parts.note: a cat is old slang for a jazz enthusiast
C stands for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: A jazz enthusiast is about to come back for a gig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to return' sends the C of CAT back behind the A.
explanation.definitionFit: An act is a turn or routine performed on stage, a performance.

clue.text: Expect prank that's involving quantity of butter

parts.note: an antic is a playful trick or caper

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so the abbreviation wraps round the butter

parts.note: i.e. stands for id est, that is
a pat is a small portion of butter

explanation.surface: Someone foresees a joke involving a dollop of butter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involving' gives IPATE; that's = i.e. is a standard convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To anticipate something is to look forward to it or foresee it, so to expect it.

clue.text: Endless dirt, looking black

indicators.note: with no end, so the final letter of the dirt word goes

parts.note: grime is ingrained dirt

explanation.surface: Ceaseless filth makes everything look dark.
explanation.definitionFit: Grim means gloomy or forbidding, so looking black in the sense of a dark outlook.

clue.text: Reluctance to move shown by train, i.e. after crash

indicators.note: after a crash things are wrecked, so the letters of train and i.e. are rearranged

explanation.surface: Passengers are slow to leave a train that has crashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after crash' is the anagram signal; 'shown by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Inertia is the tendency to remain unchanged, a lethargy or unwillingness to act.

clue.text: Article about nation's foremost swimmer

indicators.note: the article's word goes about, around, the opening letter of nation

parts.note: a leader is a newspaper's leading article, its editorial

indicators.note: the foremost letter of a word is its first

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about the country's top swimmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foremost' takes N from nation's; 'about' puts LEADER round it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to visit Hero; a famous swimmer of legend.

clue.text: A number losing height in plane, perhaps

indicators.note: losing something means it is removed from the number word

parts.note: three is a number

explanation.surface: An aircraft count drops as the planes lose altitude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes H from THREE. 'plane' is not an aircraft but the plane tree, so 'perhaps' marks an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The plane is a kind of tree, common in London streets, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Whistler initially drowned by odd percussion instrument

parts.note: a kettle whistles when it boils

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter of drowned is taken

parts.note: rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: The painter Whistler's opening was drowned out by an eccentric drummer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistler' suggests the painter but is a whistling kettle. 'initially' takes D from drowned.
explanation.definitionFit: A kettledrum, or timpani, is a large bowl-shaped drum played in orchestras.
